conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time today. I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot common mood and anxiety changes that can creep up in the first year postpartum. There’s no pass-or-fail; it’s simply a snapshot of the past seven days so we can figure out the best support for you. Everything you share is confidential, and if anything feels hard to say out loud, we can pause or adjust. When you’re ready, we’ll move through the questions at your pace. Shall we begin?

1. Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has that felt as easy as always, sometimes, not quite so much, or not at all?

Oh, I’ve definitely still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my partner makes a silly joke or when the dog does something goofy, I’ll still crack up. So I’d say “as easy as always” feels a tiny bit off, but “sometimes” covers it pretty well.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, that’s right—I’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things sometimes.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or taking the baby out in the stroller when it’s sunny. It’s not every single moment, but I’d say “sometimes,” definitely not “never.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up right after I’ve changed her or I forget to pack a burp cloth, I might think, “Oops, should’ve remembered,” but I don’t dwell on it or beat myself up. I’d say hardly ever—so “no, never” fits best.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Now and then I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing okay when she’s napping, even though she’s perfectly fine. It’s not constant—just quick little flashes—so I’d say “no, not at all” feels too strong, but it isn’t “very often” either. “Hardly ever” matches pretty well.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
I haven’t felt truly scared or panicky—no racing heart or anything like that. Maybe a brief “what-if” pops up, but it passes right away, so I’d say “no, not at all.”
Things have been getting on top of me

Not really. I mean, some moments feel hectic—like when she’s fussy and the laundry’s piled up—but I can still step back, breathe, and tick things off one by one. I wouldn’t say I’ve felt overwhelmed or that things are “getting on top of me.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, thankfully my mood hasn’t messed with my sleep. Once the baby settles for the night, I usually drift off pretty easily and stay asleep unless she wakes to feed. I haven’t felt so unhappy that it kept me up.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt sad or miserable. I get a little tired, sure, but my overall mood feels steady—I still smile when the baby grasps my finger or when my older one brings me a drawing.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried from feeling unhappy. Maybe a tear or two when I was overly tired the other night, but it wasn’t that deep unhappy kind of crying—just exhaustion.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 3: SCREENING NOTE – POSTPARTUM EPDS (EDINBURGH)

Patient-reported EPDS responses (10 items) reviewed.  

Symptoms endorsed:  
- Mild, situational “what-if” worries about infant safety (Q4), frequency described as “hardly ever.”  
- Brief tearfulness attributed to fatigue, not low mood (Q9).  

Symptoms denied:  
- Anhedonia, persistent sadness, guilt/worthlessness, sleep-mood linkage, crying spells, panic, feeling overwhelmed, self-harm ideation (Q1–3,5–8,10).  

Pattern:  
No evidence of current depressive or anxiety symptom cluster; no affective, cognitive, or safety red flags.  

Risk summary:  
- Depressive symptoms: negligible.  
- Anxiety symptoms: subclinical, isolated.  
- Self-harm: denied; no safety concern identified at screening.  

Overall screening impression:  
Responses do not indicate elevated risk for postpartum depression or anxiety; no further screening action indicated unless clinical picture changes.
